01.note: Three Sages each describe what they saw of the land's richness. Rabbi Ya'akov ben Dostai says that once, rising early on the three-mil road from Lud to Ono, he walked ankle-deep in honey oozing from fig trees. Reish Lakish says he saw the place near Tzippori 'flowing with milk and honey', sixteen mil by sixteen. Rabba bar bar Ḥana says he saw the milk-and-honey land of all Eretz Yisrael, and it was as large as the stretch from Bei Mikhsei to the fortress of Tulbanki: twenty-two parasangs long and six wide.
01.why: The Gemara is collecting reports of the bounty of the Land of Israel. Just before, Rami bar Yeḥezkel saw goats' milk and fig honey mixing in Benei Berak and called it the meaning of the verse 'a land flowing with milk and honey'; these Sages add their own sightings of that verse come true.

people.name: Rabbi Ya'akov ben Dostai
people.about: Tells of walking ankle-deep in fig honey between Lud and Ono.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Says he saw the milk-and-honey region by Tzippori.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Ḥana
people.about: Says he saw the milk-and-honey land of all Eretz Yisrael and gives its size.

terms.meaning: An ancient measure of distance, roughly a kilometer.
A larger Persian measure of distance, equal to four mil.
Hebrew for the Land of Israel.

02.note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi came to Gavla and saw grape clusters as big as calves. He asked whether those were calves standing among the vines; the locals told him they were clusters. He cried out: O earth, O earth, gather in your fruit! For whom are you producing it, for these gentiles who stand over us because of our sins? The next year Rabbi Ḥiyya came to the same place and saw clusters the size of goats. When he asked whether those were goats among the vines, the locals told him: Go away, do not do to us what your colleague did.
02.why: It belongs to a run of stories about the fruit of the Land of Israel. Like the peach that Rabbi Elazar found shrunken a year after his colleagues saw it, the grapes here are smaller the following year, and the locals blame a Sage's words.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: Sees huge grape clusters in Gavla and tells the earth to stop producing such fruit for gentile rulers.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Visits the same place the next year and is sent away by the locals.

terms.meaning: Non-Jews; here the foreign rulers of the land.

03.note: On his way up to the Land of Israel, Rabbi Zeira could not find a ferry across the Jordan, so he grabbed hold of a rope and crossed on it. A Sadducee mocked him: You hasty people, who put your mouths before your ears, are still hasty. Rabbi Zeira answered that this was a land Moses and Aaron did not merit to enter; who could say that he would merit it?
03.why: Just before, Rabbi Elazar rejoiced at each stage of being accepted in the Land of Israel; this begins a run of stories about Sages' eagerness for and love of the Land, followed by Sages who kissed its rocks and rolled in its dust.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who crosses the Jordan on a rope rather than wait to enter the Land of Israel.

terms.meaning: A member of a Jewish group that rejected the Sages' teachings; in the Talmud often a hostile questioner.
A jibe at Israel's promise at Sinai, 'We will do and we will hear', which put acting before hearing.

04.note: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin bought a maidservant, agreeing to pay in small copper coins. They did not have the coins with them, so they left a piece of silver as collateral. Later the maidservant's price went up, and the case came before Rabbi Ami. He ruled: there are no coins here and there is no silver here, so no sale has taken place.
04.why: Rav Naḥman has just ruled that a man who promises a hundred dinars for betrothal but hands over only collateral has given nothing; this purchase case shows the same principle, that collateral is not payment, applied to a sale.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The Sage who rules that the purchase was never completed.

people.name: the sons of Rav Huna bar Avin
people.about: The buyers of the maidservant.

terms.meaning: Small copper coins; a peruta is the smallest coin of value.
An item handed over as security for a debt, which remains the debtor's property.

05.note: A man was selling strings of glass beads. A woman came and said: Give me one string. He asked: If I give it to you, will you be betrothed to me? She answered: Give, give. Rav Ḥama ruled that any 'Give, give' means nothing, so she is not betrothed.
05.why: The Gemara is listing replies a woman might make when a man offers her something as betrothal, such as 'Give it to a dog' or 'to a poor person'. This opens a run of three similar cases about doubled words.

people.name: Rav Ḥama
people.about: The Sage who rules that 'Give, give' is not consent.

terms.meaning: Formally bound in the first stage of Jewish marriage, done by giving the woman an item of value that she accepts.

06.note: A man was drinking wine in a shop. A woman came in and said: Give me one cup. He asked: If I give it to you, will you be betrothed to me? She answered: Pour me a drink, pour me a drink. Rav Ḥama ruled that any such reply means nothing, so she is not betrothed.
06.why: It follows the glass-bead seller as a second case of a woman's doubled words; the Gemara then asks what happens if she says the word only once, and rules that she is still not betrothed.

people.name: Rav Ḥama
people.about: The Sage who rules that her reply is not consent.

terms.meaning: Formally bound in the first stage of Jewish marriage, done by giving the woman an item of value that she accepts.

07.note: A man was picking dates from a palm tree. A woman came and said: Throw me two. He asked: If I throw them to you, will you be betrothed to me? She answered: Throw, throw. Rav Zevid ruled that any 'Throw, throw' means nothing, so she is not betrothed.
07.why: It is the third in a run of cases about a woman repeating a word when offered betrothal; right after it the Gemara asks whether saying 'Throw' just once is different, and rules that she is not betrothed either way.

people.name: Rav Zevid
people.about: The Sage who rules that 'Throw, throw' is not consent.

terms.meaning: Formally bound in the first stage of Jewish marriage, done by giving the woman an item of value that she accepts.

08.note: A man betrothed a woman with a blue marble stone. Rav Ḥisda sat and estimated its worth: if it was worth a peruta she was betrothed, and if not she was not. The Gemara explains that Rav Ḥisda does not follow Shmuel here. The man's mother told Rav Ḥisda that on the day of the betrothal the stone was worth a peruta. He answered her: it is not in your power to forbid her to a later husband.
08.why: Shmuel has just ruled that an item worth less than a peruta here still makes a doubtful betrothal, since it may be worth more elsewhere. Rav Ḥisda's ruling goes against that, and the Gemara goes on to test it against witnesses in Idit who could say what the stone was worth.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: The Sage who values the stone and rejects the mother's claim.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage whose ruling on low-value betrothal items Rav Ḥisda does not follow.

terms.meaning: The smallest coin of value; a betrothal gift must be worth at least this much.
Formally bound in the first stage of Jewish marriage; a betrothed woman may not marry anyone else.

09.note: A man betrothed a woman with a mat woven of myrtle branches. People told him it was not worth a peruta, so he said: Let her be betrothed with the four dinars wrapped inside it. She took the mat and said nothing. Rava ruled that silence after the money has already been given means nothing. Scholars in Pum Nahara challenged his proof, Rav Aḥai answered them, and Rav Aḥa bar Rav sent the question to Ravina. Ravina replied: We never heard that objection, but you who heard it should take the possible betrothal seriously.
09.why: The Gemara is gathering cases on when a woman's silence counts as agreeing to betrothal; the next case, a woman whose snatched belt is handed back to her, raises the same question.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rules that silence after the money is given is not consent.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: The Sage in whose name the scholars of Pum Nahara challenge Rava.

people.name: Rav Aḥai
people.about: Answers that challenge: not every woman knows the law.

people.name: Rav Aḥa bar Rav
people.about: Sends the question to Ravina.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Replies that those who heard the objection should be concerned about a betrothal.

terms.meaning: The smallest coin of value; a betrothal gift must be worth at least this much.
A teaching of the early Sages that was left out of the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

09.flag: The STORY runs from the myrtle-mat case (12b) into the Gemara's legal argument on 13a, starting mid-sentence; segments 5-7 are debate about a baraita rather than part of the story.

10.note: A woman was selling belts. A man came and snatched one from her. She said: Give it to me. He asked: If I give it to you, will you be betrothed to me? She took it and said nothing. Rav Naḥman ruled that she can say: Yes, I took it, but what I took was my own.
10.why: It follows the debate on whether a woman's silence counts as consent. Rava then challenges Rav Naḥman with a teaching that a woman is betrothed with a coin snatched from her, and Rav Naḥman answers that there the couple had already arranged the marriage.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Rules that taking back her own belt in silence does not betroth her.

terms.meaning: Formally bound in the first stage of Jewish marriage, done by giving the woman an item of value that she accepts.

11.note: Rabbi Yehuda from India was a convert with no heirs. When he fell ill, Mar Zutra came to visit him and saw that he was getting much worse. Mar Zutra told Rabbi Yehuda's slave: Take off my shoes and carry them to my house, so that the slave's service would make him Mar Zutra's. The Gemara gives two views of the slave. Some say he was an adult: one man departed to death and the other to life. Others say he was a minor, and Mar Zutra did not follow Abba Shaul, who held that anyone may take a dead convert's minor slaves.
11.why: The Gemara has just said a master acquires a slave when the slave does labor for him, such as carrying him. Mar Zutra has the slave carry his shoes, an act of service, while the owner is still alive.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda from India
people.about: A convert with no heirs, who falls ill and is dying.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: Visits him and has the slave carry his shoes so as to acquire him.

people.name: Abba Shaul
people.about: A Sage whose view on a dead convert's minor slaves Mar Zutra did not follow.

terms.meaning: A person who joined the Jewish people. A convert with no Jewish heirs leaves property that the first person to take it acquires.
A teaching of the early Sages that was left out of the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

12.note: The elders of Nezonya stopped coming to Rav Ḥisda's lectures, and he sent Rav Hamnuna to ostracize them. Rav Hamnuna asked them why they stayed away. They said Rav Ḥisda had not answered a question of theirs, so Rav Hamnuna invited them to ask him. They asked: if a master castrates his slave, does the slave go free, as he would for a visible injury? Rav Hamnuna did not know. They mocked his name: not Hamnuna, a hot fish, but Karnuna, a cold one. He went back to Rav Ḥisda, who told him the answer was in a teaching they could have cited, and began to quote it.
12.why: The Gemara is listing injuries that free a slave when his master causes them, like an eye or an extra finger. The elders' question adds castration, and the teaching Rav Ḥisda points to lists the body's extremities and, in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view, castration as well.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: A Sage whose lectures the elders of Nezonya stop attending.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: Sent by Rav Ḥisda to ostracize the elders; cannot answer their question.

people.name: the elders of Nezonya
people.about: Local scholars who stay away from Rav Ḥisda's lectures.

terms.meaning: To place someone under a ban that cuts them off from the community until they make amends.
A visible injury to a slave's body; a master who causes one must set the slave free.
A teaching from the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.
In the laws of skin disease, a patch of healthy flesh inside a diseased spot that makes a person ritually impure.

13.note: Rabbi Elazar told of a Madonite in Jerusalem who owned a great deal of movable property and wanted to give it away. The Sages told him the only way was to transfer it along with a piece of land. So he bought a beit sela of land near Jerusalem and said: This northern part goes to so-and-so, and with it a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels. Then he died, and the Sages carried out his words.
13.why: The Gemara is asking whether movable goods must be piled on the land to be acquired along with it. This case is brought as proof that they need not be, since a hundred sheep could not fit on so small a plot. The Gemara rejects the proof by reading 'sela' as rock-hard land, not a tiny one.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: The Sage who tells the story.

people.name: the Madonite
people.about: A man in Jerusalem who gives away his goods through a small plot of land before he dies.

terms.meaning: Goods that can be moved, such as animals and barrels, as opposed to land.
A plot of land, apparently the size of a sela coin; the Gemara later reads it otherwise.

14.note: Rav Yehuda reported in Rav's name the case of a man in Jerusalem, sick by one account and healthy by another, who owned a great deal of movable property and wanted to give it away. The Sages told him the only way was to transfer it along with land. He bought a small plot near Jerusalem and said: This square handbreadth goes to so-and-so, and with it a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels. Then he died, and the Sages carried out his words.
14.why: This is a second attempt to prove that goods need not be piled on the land to pass with it. The Gemara answers that the gift may have been money, which fits on a tiny plot, and then argues over why he could not have used another method.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Reports the case in Rav's name.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage whose account Rav Yehuda passes on.

terms.meaning: Goods that can be moved, such as animals and barrels, as opposed to land.
A measure of about the width of a hand, roughly 8 to 10 cm.
Two sides of an argument over how a dying person may give property away; the two accounts of the man's health match their two views.

15.note: Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov sent his son Rav Ya'akov to study with Abaye. When the son came home, his father saw that his learning was not sharp, and said: I am better than you; you stay home and I will go. Abaye heard he was coming. A demon haunted Abaye's study hall, so dangerous that even two people entering by day were harmed. Abaye told the townspeople not to give Rav Aḥa lodging, since perhaps a miracle would happen. Rav Aḥa slept in the study hall, and the demon appeared to him as a serpent with seven heads. With every bow he made, one head fell off. The next day he told them: If no miracle had happened, you would have put me in danger.
15.why: A teaching of the Sages says that when father and son both want to study, the father comes first, unless the son is quick and sharp. This story is told as an example: the father judges his son not sharp enough and goes to study himself.

people.name: Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov
people.about: A father who goes to study in place of his son and defeats the demon.

people.name: Rav Ya'akov
people.about: Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov's son, sent to study with Abaye.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Head of the study hall, who arranges for Rav Aḥa to spend the night there.

terms.meaning: A harmful spirit; the Talmud treats demons as real dangers in certain places.

16.note: Rav Ḥisda kept praising Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna as a great man. Rav Huna asked that he be sent to him. When Rav Hamnuna arrived, Rav Huna saw that he wore no head cloth, as scholars did, and asked why. Rav Hamnuna said it was because he was not married. Rav Huna turned his face away and said: See that you do not see my face until you marry. Further sayings follow: someone says he would tell the Satan 'an arrow in your eye', and Rava tells Rabbi Natan bar Ami to marry off his son while he still has authority over him, between sixteen and twenty-two or eighteen and twenty-four.
16.why: The Gemara has just asked whether a man should study Torah first or marry first, and Shmuel ruled to marry first. Rav Huna's rebuke of the unmarried scholar shows that ruling put into practice.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Praises Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Rebukes Rav Hamnuna for being unmarried.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A praised scholar who is not yet married.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Advises Rabbi Natan bar Ami to find his son a wife.

people.name: Rabbi Natan bar Ami
people.about: Receives Rava's advice about his son.

terms.meaning: Here, the evil inclination, the urge to sin.

16.flag: Segment 5 (30a) begins mid-statement with 'I would say to the Satan', a saying whose speaker and start are missing, and then moves to Rava's advice on when to marry off a son; it is not part of the Rav Hamnuna story.

17.note: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba came upon Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi with a cheap covering thrown over his head, hurrying a child to the synagogue to study. He asked what all the rush was about. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi answered with a verse: is it a small thing that 'make them known to your sons' stands next to 'the day you stood before the Lord your God at Horeb'? From then on Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba would not eat his morning meal until he had read with his child and added to his lessons. Rabba bar Rav Huna would not eat until he had brought his child to the study hall.
17.why: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi has just taught that whoever teaches his grandson Torah is credited as if he received it at Mount Sinai. Here he is seen acting on his own teaching, and it changes the habits of others.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba
people.about: Questions Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's haste and then adopts the practice himself.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: Rushes to bring a child to study, citing a verse.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: Also would not eat before bringing his child to the study hall.

terms.meaning: Another name for Mount Sinai, where the Torah was given.
Here an idiom for eating the morning meal.

18.note: The Sages asked Rav Ulla how far one must go in honoring father and mother. He told them about Dama ben Netina, a gentile in Ashkelon. The Sages wanted to buy goods from him at a profit of six hundred thousand gold dinars, but the key was under his sleeping father's head, and he would not disturb him. In a second version, told by Rabbi Eliezer, the goods were precious stones for the High Priest's ephod, and Rav Kahana put the profit at eight hundred thousand. The next year God gave Dama his reward: a red heifer was born in his herd. When the Sages came for it, he said he knew they would pay any price, but he asked only the money he had lost by honoring his father.
18.why: Just before, Ulla taught that the nations accepted God's words once they heard 'Honor your father and your mother'. The question of how far that duty goes leads to this story, and afterward Rabbi Ḥanina argues that one who is commanded and obeys is greater than a gentile like Dama.

people.name: Rav Ulla
people.about: Asked how far honoring parents goes; tells of Dama ben Netina.

people.name: Dama ben Netina
people.about: A gentile in Ashkelon who gives up a great profit rather than wake his father.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: Tells a second version of the story.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Teaches that the profit was eight hundred thousand.

people.name: the Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, who rewards Dama with a red heifer.

terms.meaning: An embroidered garment worn by the High Priest, set with precious stones.
A rare all-red cow whose ashes were needed for ritual purification, making it extremely valuable.
A non-Jew, who is not commanded by the Torah to honor his parents.

19.note: Rav Dimi reported that once Dama ben Netina was wearing a cloak of gold and sitting among the nobles of Rome. His mother came, tore the cloak off him, struck him on the head and spat in his face, and he did not shame her.
19.why: The Gemara has been telling of Dama ben Netina as the model of honoring parents. After his honor of his father, this account shows how far he went in honoring his mother.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: Brings this account of Dama ben Netina.

people.name: Dama ben Netina
people.about: A gentile whose patience with his mother is the model of honoring parents.

19.flag: Segment 5 ('and this action brings him to the life of the World-to-Come', 31b) is the end of Avimi's separate teaching about sons and fathers, not part of the Dama ben Netina story.

20.note: Rabbi Abbahu said that his son Avimi was one who truly kept the commandment of honoring parents. Avimi had five sons ordained as rabbis in his father's lifetime, yet whenever Rabbi Abbahu called at the gate, Avimi ran to open it himself, calling 'Yes, yes' until he got there. Once his father asked him for water, and by the time Avimi brought it he had dozed off. Avimi stood bent over him until he woke. This helped him, and he was able to expound the psalm 'A song of Asaph'.
20.why: Avimi has just taught that one son may feed his father pheasant and lose the World to Come while another sets him to grinding and earns it; his father now holds Avimi up as the son who honors properly.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: Avimi's father, who praises him.

people.name: Avimi
people.about: Rabbi Abbahu's son, who serves his father with great care.

terms.meaning: Formally authorized as rabbis to give rulings in Jewish law.
The Torah's command 'Honor your father and your mother'.
